Q3889.w: A city on red cliffs along a wide bay, with a suspension bridge across the estuary and a large island near the bay's mouth.
f: The Maputo–Katembe Bridge, opened in 2018, has a main span of about 680 metres.
Inhaca Island, at the mouth of the bay, is ringed by coral reefs and seagrass meadows.
Maputo lies less than 100 km from the borders of both South Africa and Eswatini.

q.q: What was Maputo called until 1976?

Q1763.t: The largest city beyond the Arctic Circle
Q1763.s: Murmansk stretches along the eastern shore of the Kola Bay, a long, fjord-like inlet running north to the Barents Sea. It is the largest city in the world north of the Arctic Circle. Thanks to the last warm reach of the North Atlantic Current, its port stays free of ice all winter, while the lakes and tundra around it freeze solid.
Q1763.w: A long city on the hilly east shore of a narrow, fjord-like bay, surrounded by low tundra dotted with lakes.
f: The polar night here lasts about 40 days, from early December to mid-January.
The midnight sun shines over Murmansk from late May to late July.
Murmansk was founded in 1916.

q.q: What keeps Murmansk's port free of ice in winter?

ne-pp-1159150693.t: Russia's first seaport, on a great northern delta
ne-pp-1159150693.s: Arkhangelsk lies where the Northern Dvina fans out into a broad delta of channels and islands before meeting the White Sea. Endless dark taiga surrounds it. Founded in 1584 around the monastery of the Archangel Michael, it was for over a century Russia's main gateway to the sea, until Saint Petersburg took over. In winter the frozen river becomes a white highway.
ne-pp-1159150693.w: A long city along a wide river splitting into many channels just before a large bay, surrounded by dark forest.
f: The scientist Mikhail Lomonosov was born in 1711 near Kholmogory, upstream on the Dvina.
Ice covers the sea near the city for roughly half the year.
The Solovetsky Islands, a UNESCO site, lie in the White Sea about 230 km to the west.

q.q: Which river forms a delta at Arkhangelsk?

Q891.t: Where the Oka pours into the Volga
Q891.s: Nizhny Novgorod stands at one of Russia's great river meetings: the Oka flows into the Volga right at the city's heart. The old town sits high on the steep right bank, looking across the water to a low, forested plain on the far side. The city was founded in 1221 to guard this junction of river routes.
Q891.w: Two wide rivers meeting at a sharp point, with the city on high wooded bluffs and flat forest across the Volga.
f: A cable car across the Volga links the city with the town of Bor, about 3.6 km away.
From 1817 the city hosted a famous summer trade fair, one of the largest in the Russian Empire.
The Volga, which flows past the city, is Europe's longest river at about 3,500 km.

q.q: Which river joins the Volga at Nizhny Novgorod?

Q914.t: A city stretched for dozens of kilometres along the Volga
Q914.s: Volgograd is one of the longest cities in Europe: a narrow ribbon along the high western bank of the Volga, running for more than 60 km. Across the river lies a completely different world, the green Volga–Akhtuba floodplain, laced with channels, lakes and woods. At the city's southern end, the Volga–Don Canal sets off west towards the Don.
Q914.w: A long, narrow city on the west bank of the broad Volga, facing a green, channel-laced floodplain on the east.
f: The Volga–Don Canal, about 100 km long, links the Volga with the Don and so with the Black Sea.
A dam just north of the city holds back the Volgograd Reservoir, which is about 540 km long.
The Volga–Akhtuba floodplain opposite the city is protected as a nature park.

q.q: What was Volgograd's original name?

Q911.t: A city on a ridge between two winding rivers
Q911.s: Ufa stretches along a long, high ridge between two rivers, the Belaya and the Ufa, which wind below it in wide loops before they meet. To the east the land rises gently towards the Southern Urals. The city is the capital of Bashkortostan, a region known for its forested hills and its honey from wild bees.
Q911.w: A long city on a high ridge squeezed between two meandering rivers, with forested hills to the east.
f: The Belaya, Ufa's main river, is the largest tributary of the Kama.
In Bashkortostan's forests, honey is still gathered from wild bees nesting in hollow trees.
The city grew from a Russian fortress founded in 1574.

q.q: Ufa stands where the river Ufa meets which other river?

Q894.t: Where the Volga swings round a loop of wooded hills
Q894.s: Samara lies on the left bank of the Volga beside one of the river's most dramatic features, the Samara Bend: the Volga swings east in a huge loop around the forested Zhiguli Mountains. From above, the loop and its dark wooded hills are unmistakable. The city stretches for kilometres along the river, which is more than a kilometre wide here.
Q894.w: A long city on the east bank of the broad Volga, facing the dark, forested hills inside the river's great loop.
f: The Zhiguli Mountains inside the loop are protected as a nature reserve and a national park.
Samara was founded in 1586 as a fortress guarding the Volga trade route.
Upstream, the Volga widens into the Kuybyshev Reservoir, the largest reservoir in Europe.

q.q: Which hills does the Volga loop around near Samara?

Q900.t: A city where the Volga spreads wide as a sea
Q900.s: Kazan stands on the left bank of the Volga where the little Kazanka river flows in, and here the Volga, swollen by a reservoir downstream, is several kilometres wide. The white-walled kremlin sits on a hill above the confluence. For centuries Russian and Tatar, Christian and Muslim cultures have met here, and it is the capital of Tatarstan.
Q900.w: A large city on the east bank of a very wide stretch of the Volga, split by a smaller river flowing in from the north-east.
f: The Kazan Kremlin has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2000.
Some 70 km downstream, the Kama, the Volga's largest tributary, joins it.
Kazan celebrated its 1,000th anniversary in 2005.

q.q: Which small river flows into the Volga at Kazan's kremlin?

Q2449.t: An old Indian Ocean trading port among white dunes
Q2449.s: Mogadishu lines the Indian Ocean coast of the Horn of Africa, a pale city backed by sand dunes, with reefs just offshore. For a thousand years it was a trading port linking Africa with Arabia, Persia and India. When the traveller Ibn Battuta visited in 1331, he described a very large and wealthy town whose cloth was sent as far as Egypt.
Q2449.w: A pale city along a straight surf coast, backed by sandy dunes, with the green valley of the Shabelle inland to the west.
f: Mogadishu lies only about 230 km north of the equator.
The Shabelle River passes within about 30 km of the city but never reaches the sea.
In the Middle Ages the Sultanate of Mogadishu minted its own coins.

q.q: Which famous traveller visited Mogadishu in 1331?

Q3826.t: A city threaded between dark mountains and the sea
Q3826.s: Muscat doesn't sprawl like other Gulf capitals: it is threaded through a string of coves and valleys between the rugged Hajar Mountains and the Gulf of Oman. The dark brown rock of those mountains is ancient ocean floor, pushed up onto land. In the old harbour, two Portuguese forts from the 16th century still guard the entrance.
Q3826.w: A long string of white districts in valleys and coves between dark, jagged mountains and a blue sea.
f: The Semail ophiolite, the dark rock around Muscat, is one of the largest exposed slabs of oceanic crust on Earth.
Forts Jalali and Mirani were built by the Portuguese in the 1580s.
For centuries Muscat's sheltered cove served ships trading between Arabia, India and East Africa.

q.q: What are Muscat's dark mountains largely made of?

Q465022.t: Nigeria's coal city below a green escarpment
Q465022.s: Enugu lies at the foot of the Udi Hills, a steep, green escarpment rising on its western side in south-eastern Nigeria. Coal was found in those hills in 1909, and the town grew up around the mines, earning the nickname 'Coal City'. From above, look for the city nestled against the ridge, with rolling, wooded farmland all around.
Q465022.w: A city at the foot of a steep, green escarpment on its west side, amid rolling, wooded hills.
f: Coal was discovered in the Udi Hills in 1909, and mining began a few years later.
The Udi Plateau rises a few hundred metres above the plain around the city.

q.q: What does the Igbo name Enugu mean?

Q336350.t: Capital of a 19th-century caliphate, on a Sahel river
Q336350.s: Sokoto lies in the far north-west of Nigeria, where the Sokoto and Rima rivers meet on a broad, flat floodplain. In the rainy season the valley floor turns green with rice and vegetables; the rest of the year, dusty savanna stretches to the horizon. The city was founded in 1809 as the capital of the Sokoto Caliphate, one of Africa's largest 19th-century states.
Q336350.w: A low, dusty city on a flat plain beside a broad river valley, with green fields along the water.
f: The Sokoto Caliphate stretched from present-day Burkina Faso to Cameroon.
Sokoto is one of Nigeria's hottest cities, with April afternoons often above 40 °C.
The Sultan of Sokoto is still regarded as a spiritual leader by many Nigerian Muslims.

q.q: Who founded the Sokoto Caliphate?

Q915.t: The city that gave its name to a geological age
Q915.s: Perm stretches for kilometres along the Kama, a broad river that widens into a reservoir just upstream. Endless taiga surrounds it, and to the east the first low ridges of the Urals begin. In 1841 the Scottish geologist Roderick Murchison studied the rocks of this region and named a whole period of Earth's history after it: the Permian.
Q915.w: A long city on both banks of a wide river, with a reservoir upstream and dark forest in every direction.
f: The Permian period, roughly 299 to 252 million years ago, ended with the largest mass extinction in Earth's history.
Perm began in 1723 as a copper-smelting works.
The city stretches for about 70 km along the Kama.

q.q: Which geological period is named after the Perm region?

Q335548.t: A highland town near a giant iron meteorite
Q335548.s: Mbeya sits in a high valley in Tanzania's Southern Highlands, about 1,700 metres up, with the steep Mbeya Range rising right behind it. The land around is intensely green, a patchwork of tea, coffee and maize on rich volcanic soils. South-west of the town, a lump of iron from space weighing around 16 tonnes still rests where it fell.
Q335548.w: A town in a green valley at the foot of a steep mountain range, surrounded by a patchwork of highland farms.
f: The Mbozi meteorite, some 50 km south-west of Mbeya, is one of the largest meteorites ever found.
Mbeya Peak, the highest point of the range above the town, rises to about 2,800 metres.
Further east, the Kitulo Plateau is so rich in wild orchids that it is called the 'Garden of God'.

q.q: What giant object lies at Mbozi, near Mbeya?

Q3935.t: A highland capital in the heart of a dry land
Q3935.s: Windhoek lies in a basin in Namibia's central highlands, about 1,650 metres up, framed by the Auas Mountains to the south and the Eros hills to the north. Around it stretches dry, thorny savanna, brown for much of the year. Water is so precious here that since 1968 the city has turned wastewater directly into drinking water, a world first.
Q3935.w: A compact city in a bowl of low, rugged hills on dry, brown highland savanna.
f: Namibia's Atlantic coast lies about 300 km to the west.
The Auas Mountains south of the city rise to about 2,480 metres, among the highest in Namibia.
Hot springs once bubbled up in the valley, drawing the first settlers.

q.q: What has Windhoek done with its wastewater since 1968?
x: Used it to cool a power plant

Q986336.t: A quiet farm town beside the heaviest meteorite on Earth
Q986336.s: Grootfontein is a small town in the bushland of northern Namibia, named after a large spring that drew settlers and cattle herders. The surprise lies about 20 km west, on a farm: the Hoba meteorite, a slab of iron weighing around 60 tonnes, the largest known on Earth. It is so heavy that it has never been moved from where it landed.
Q986336.w: A small town in green, bushy savanna, with low dolomite hills and farmland around it.
f: The Hoba meteorite fell less than 80,000 years ago and was found by a farmer in 1920.
Grootfontein means 'big spring' in Afrikaans.
The dolomite country around the town hides sinkhole lakes, such as Otjikoto near Tsumeb.

q.q: What record-breaking object lies near Grootfontein?

Q2222874.t: A spice-island port of coral stone and turquoise water
Q2222874.s: Zanzibar City lies on the west coast of Unguja, the main island of the Zanzibar archipelago, facing the African mainland across a channel of turquoise shallows and reefs. Its old heart, Stone Town, is a maze of coral-stone houses. In 1840 the Sultan of Oman made it his capital, and cloves grown on the island were shipped around the world.
Q2222874.w: A town on the west coast of a flat green island, fringed by turquoise reefs and sandbanks, with the mainland to the west.
f: Stone Town has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2000.
Freddie Mercury was born in Stone Town in 1946.
In the 19th century Zanzibar was the world's leading producer of cloves.

q.q: Which spice made Zanzibar famous in the 19th century?

Q8818.t: A green river of parkland through an orange-grove city
Q8818.s: Valencia lies on a flat coastal plain by the Mediterranean, surrounded by the huerta, a patchwork of irrigated orchards and fields. Look for a long green ribbon curving through the city: the old bed of the river Turia, turned into a park after the river was diverted to the south. Just south of the city glints the Albufera, a lagoon ringed by rice paddies.
Q8818.w: A large city on a flat coast, with a green park snaking through it and a big shallow lagoon and rice fields to the south.
f: The Turia Gardens, laid out in the old riverbed, run for about 9 km through the city.
The rice fields around the Albufera lagoon are the home of paella.
The Romans founded Valencia in 138 BC.

q.q: Which dish was born in the rice fields around Valencia?

Q3787.t: A planned capital among giant granite domes
Q3787.s: Abuja was built from scratch near the geographic centre of Nigeria and became the capital in 1991. From above, look for its broad avenues fanning out below Aso Rock, a bare granite dome about 400 metres high on the city's eastern edge. The hilly savanna around it is studded with more of these great rounded rocks.
Q3787.w: A spacious planned city of wide avenues at the foot of a big bare granite dome, in hilly green savanna.
f: Zuma Rock, a huge granite monolith about 40 km west of the city, appears on Nigeria's 100-naira note.
The city's master plan was drawn up in the late 1970s.
Abuja lies in the Federal Capital Territory, carved out so the capital would belong to no single state.

q.q: Which city did Abuja replace as Nigeria's capital in 1991?

Q3739.t: A river-mouth capital facing a maze of islands
Q3739.s: Bissau lies on the wide estuary of the Geba River, where muddy water, mangroves and tidal flats blur the line between land and sea. Offshore spreads the Bijagós archipelago, a scatter of dozens of low, green islands and sandbanks. The tides are strong, and at low water vast banks of mud and sand appear. The Portuguese built a fort here in 1687.
Q3739.w: A city on a broad, muddy estuary lined with mangroves, with a scatter of low green islands out to sea.
f: The Bijagós archipelago has about 88 islands and islets, only around 20 of them permanently inhabited.
On the Bijagós, hippos swim in salt water between the islands.
The Geba estuary is so broad at Bissau that it looks more like an arm of the sea than a river.

q.q: Which archipelago lies off the coast at Bissau?

Q2656.t: A city in a golden shell between mountains and sea
Q2656.s: Palermo fills a broad bay on Sicily's north coast, set in a crescent of bare mountains. The plain it stands on is called the Conca d'Oro, the 'golden shell', after the citrus groves that once covered it. To the north, the limestone headland of Monte Pellegrino juts out into the sea. Phoenicians founded the city in the 8th century BC.
Q2656.w: A city on a plain curving around a bay, ringed by bare mountains, with a big rocky headland on its northern side.
f: Goethe called Monte Pellegrino the most beautiful promontory in the world.
Palermo's Arab-Norman buildings became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2015.
The Phoenicians called the city Ziz, usually translated as 'flower'.

q.q: What is the plain around Palermo called?

Q3805.t: A white-stone city spilling over many hills
Q3805.s: Amman spreads over a tangle of steep hills on the edge of the desert plateau, and from above it looks almost entirely white, since most buildings are faced with pale limestone. To the west the land drops away into the Jordan Valley and the Dead Sea, some 40 km off. In Greco-Roman times the city was called Philadelphia.
Q3805.w: A pale, almost white city draped over steep hills, with the deep trench of the Jordan Valley and the Dead Sea to the west.
f: The shore of the Dead Sea, about 430 metres below sea level, is the lowest land on Earth.
Amman's Roman theatre, cut into a hillside, seated about 6,000 people.
The city grew on the site of Rabbath Ammon, capital of the ancient Ammonites.

q.q: What was Amman called in Greco-Roman times?

Q216.t: A baroque city among forested hills and river bends
Q216.s: Vilnius lies where the little Vilnia joins the winding Neris, among wooded hills that give the city a surprisingly green look from above. Its old town, one of the largest in Eastern Europe, is packed with baroque church towers. The city is first mentioned in 1323, in letters of Grand Duke Gediminas inviting merchants and craftsmen to settle here.
Q216.w: A green, hilly city on a looping river, with forests reaching right into town and many lakes to the west.
f: The Old Town of Vilnius has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1994.
In 1989 French geographers placed the geographic centre of Europe about 26 km north of Vilnius.
Trakai, with its island castle on a lake, lies less than 30 km to the west.

q.q: Which river does the Vilnia flow into at Vilnius?

Q1773.t: A Hanseatic port where a great river meets the gulf
Q1773.s: Riga stands on the Daugava a few kilometres before it flows into the Gulf of Riga, a broad, shallow bay of the Baltic. From above, the wide river divides the compact old town on the east bank from newer districts on the west, and pine forests and bogs close in all around. Bishop Albert founded the city in 1201, and it became a leading Hanseatic port.
Q1773.w: A city on a wide river just before it enters a broad bay, with sandy coast and dark pine forest along the shore.
f: About a third of the buildings in central Riga are Art Nouveau, one of the densest collections anywhere.
The historic centre of Riga has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1997.
West of the city, the resort of Jūrmala stretches for more than 30 km along a sandy beach.

q.q: Which river flows through Riga?

Q225641.t: An island port wrapped in two deep creeks
Q225641.s: Mombasa's old heart is an island, a low coral block wedged between two deep inlets that reach into the Kenyan coast. On one side, Kilindini Harbour shelters one of East Africa's biggest ports; on the other, the old town faces Tudor Creek. Offshore, a line of white surf marks the fringing reef. For centuries this was a key port of the Swahili coast.
Q225641.w: A small island tucked between two winding creeks on a green coast, with white surf breaking on the reef offshore.
f: Fort Jesus, begun in 1593, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Vasco da Gama called at Mombasa in 1498 on his way to India.
The island is joined to the mainland by causeways and bridges, and to the south coast by ferry.

q.q: Who built Fort Jesus in Mombasa in the 1590s?

Q3909.t: The lowland capital of a kingdom in the sky
Q3909.s: Maseru sits on the Caledon River, right on Lesotho's western border, and even this 'lowland' capital is about 1,600 metres above the sea. Lesotho is completely surrounded by South Africa. From above, look east: the land climbs into the Maloti Mountains, where most of the country lies above 1,800 metres, often dusted with snow in winter.
Q3909.w: A town beside a narrow river border, with flat farmland to the west and folded, bare mountains rising to the east.
f: Lesotho's lowest point, about 1,400 metres, is the highest 'lowest point' of any country.
Maseru's name means 'red sandstones' in Sesotho.
Thaba Bosiu, the flat-topped mountain stronghold of King Moshoeshoe I, lies about 25 km to the east.

q.q: Which country completely surrounds Lesotho?

Q3915.t: A hill city among rice paddies on the Great Red Island
Q3915.s: Antananarivo sprawls over a long granite ridge and the hills around it in the middle of Madagascar, about 1,300 metres up. Between the hills, bright green rice paddies still fill the valleys right inside the city, and the soil around is a striking red. The name means 'city of the thousand', said to recall a thousand warriors who guarded it.
Q3915.w: A hilly city with a long ridge at its centre, bright green rice paddies in the valleys and red earth all around.
f: The Rova, the old royal palace compound, crowns the highest hill in the city.
Lake Anosy in the city centre is ringed by jacaranda trees that bloom purple in spring.
Madagascar's red laterite soils earned it the nickname 'the Great Red Island'.

q.q: What does the name Antananarivo mean?

Q456.t: Two rivers meeting at the tip of a narrow peninsula
Q456.s: Lyon is built around a meeting of rivers. The broad, fast Rhône, coming from the Alps, and the calmer Saône, from the north, run side by side through the city, enclosing a long, narrow peninsula before they join at its southern tip. West of the Saône rises the hill of Fourvière. The Romans founded Lugdunum here in 43 BC.
Q456.w: Two rivers running side by side through a big city, a long thin strip of land between them, joining at a point to the south.
f: Lugdunum was a capital of Roman Gaul, and the emperor Claudius was born here.
The historic centre of Lyon has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1998.
From the 16th to the 19th century Lyon was Europe's great silk-weaving city.

q.q: Which two rivers meet at Lyon?

Q1004822.t: A river port near the top of the Congo's great arc
Q1004822.s: Bumba sits on the north bank of the Congo, near the top of the great arc the river draws across Central Africa. Here the Congo is a braided giant, several kilometres wide and dotted with long wooded islands, flowing through unbroken rainforest. From above, the brown river and the dark green canopy stretch to every horizon.
Q1004822.w: A small town on the north bank of a huge, braided brown river full of wooded islands, amid endless rainforest.
f: The Congo crosses the equator twice on its long arc through Central Africa.
Only the Amazon carries more water to the sea than the Congo.
Around Bumba the river reaches the northernmost part of its course.

q.q: How many times does the Congo River cross the equator?

Q3659.t: A Sahel capital where two rivers meet on a border
Q3659.s: N'Djamena stands where the Logone flows into the Chari, on a flat plain at the southern edge of the Sahel. Across the Logone lies Cameroon, so close that the two countries face each other over the water. The combined river flows on north-west to Lake Chad, a shallow lake that swells and shrinks dramatically with the seasons and the years.
Q3659.w: A flat city at a river confluence, with a smaller town across the water and floodplains and dry savanna around.
f: The Chari river system supplies about 90 percent of the water reaching Lake Chad.
The city was founded in 1900 as Fort-Lamy.
The southern shore of Lake Chad lies roughly 100 km north-west of the city.

q.q: Which lake does the Chari feed, north-west of N'Djamena?

Q242587.t: An old sultanate capital on a caravan road
Q242587.s: Abéché lies on the dry plateau of eastern Chad, a low, sand-coloured town among scattered rocky hills and seasonal riverbeds. From 1850 it was the capital of the Sultanate of Wadai, a powerful Sahel state. Caravans once set out from here across the Sahara to the Mediterranean coast at Benghazi, some 2,000 km away.
Q242587.w: A small, dusty town among low rocky hills and dry, sandy riverbeds on a flat, brown plateau.
f: The earlier Wadai capital, Ouara, lies in ruins some 50 km to the north.
Most of the year's rain falls in July and August, briefly turning the wadis into rivers.

q.q: Abéché was the capital of which sultanate?

Q3818.t: An island capital beneath a 3,000-metre volcano
Q3818.s: Malabo lies on the north coast of Bioko, a lush volcanic island in the Gulf of Guinea, separated from the rest of its country on the mainland. Behind it rises Pico Basilé, a forested volcano topping 3,000 metres and often capped in cloud. The city's harbour curves inside the rim of an old volcanic crater, partly flooded by the sea.
Q3818.w: A small city on the north shore of a green volcanic island, with a huge forested peak rising behind it.
f: Pico Basilé, at about 3,010 metres, is the highest point of Equatorial Guinea.
Bioko lies less than 40 km off the coast of Cameroon.
Malabo is one of the few capitals set on an island apart from its country's mainland.

q.q: What was Malabo called when the British founded it in 1827?

Q130514.t: Ancient Thebes, split by the Nile between life and death
Q130514.s: Luxor straddles the Nile in a narrow green valley between bare desert cliffs. On the east bank, where the sun rises, lie the town and the vast temples of Karnak and Luxor. On the west bank, beyond the fields, the land rises to dry limestone hills hiding the Valley of the Kings, where pharaohs of the New Kingdom were buried.
Q130514.w: A green strip on both banks of the Nile, a town on the east side and pale desert cliffs rising sharply on the west.
f: As Thebes, this was Egypt's capital for much of the New Kingdom, more than 3,000 years ago.
The Karnak temple complex is one of the largest religious sites ever built.
Ancient Thebes and its necropolis became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1979.

q.q: What did the ancient Greeks call the city at Luxor?

Q3642.t: A modernist city on the rim of a great escarpment
Q3642.s: Asmara sits on the Eritrean highlands at about 2,300 metres, near the edge of a dramatic escarpment. Just to the east, the land plunges more than 2,000 metres towards the hot Red Sea coast in only a few dozen kilometres. The city's streets are lined with early 20th-century modernist buildings, and in 2017 UNESCO listed it as a modernist African city.
Q3642.w: A compact city on a high plateau, beside the edge of a steep, deeply cut escarpment falling east towards the Red Sea.
f: A narrow-gauge railway winds down the escarpment from Asmara to the port of Massawa.
Thanks to its altitude, Asmara has mild temperatures all year despite lying in the tropics.
Asmara's name is often explained as 'they united them', after four villages that joined together.

q.q: For which style of architecture is Asmara UNESCO-listed?

Q1435.t: A city between a wooded mountain and the Sava
Q1435.s: Zagreb spreads south from the slopes of Medvednica, a forested mountain rising just north of the city, down to the broad plain of the Sava. The historic core sits on the lower hills; newer districts stretch across the flat land beyond the river. The two medieval towns of Gradec and Kaptol were united as one city in 1850.
Q1435.w: A city between a dark, forested mountain to the north and a river crossing the flat plain to the south.
f: Sljeme, the summit of Medvednica, rises to about 1,030 metres.
In the Lower Town, a U-shaped chain of parks and squares is known as the 'Green Horseshoe'.
The Sava, flowing past the city, joins the Danube at Belgrade.

q.q: Which river flows through Zagreb?

Q1770.t: A medieval Hanseatic town on a limestone bay
Q1770.s: Tallinn sits on a wide bay of the Gulf of Finland, with wooded islands out in the water and Helsinki about 80 km across the sea. Its medieval old town, one of the best preserved in Northern Europe, clusters around Toompea, a limestone hill that belongs to the Baltic Klint, a long coastal escarpment. As Reval, it was a prosperous Hanseatic port.
Q1770.w: A compact city curving around a broad bay with a few wooded islands, and flat, forested coast stretching east and west.
f: The historic centre of Tallinn has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1997.
The Baltic Klint, a limestone escarpment, runs for more than 1,000 km from Sweden into Russia.
Tallinn's name is often explained as 'Danish town', recalling Danish rule in the 13th century.

q.q: What was Tallinn's old Hanseatic name?

Q261887.t: A river town where grassy plateaus meet forested valleys
Q261887.s: Kikwit lies on the Kwilu River in south-western Congo, a busy regional town in a landscape of grassy plateaus sliced by deep, forested valleys. From above, look for the striking pattern: pale savanna on the high ground and dark green ribbons of gallery forest along every stream. The Kwilu flows north towards the Kasai and, eventually, the Congo.
Q261887.w: A town on a winding river, with pale grassy plateaus and dark green strips of forest lining the valleys.
f: The Kwilu joins the Kwango, which feeds the Kasai, one of the Congo's largest tributaries.
The country around Kikwit has long been known for its oil palms.

q.q: Which river flows through Kikwit?

Q211073.t: A rocky river port where the ocean ships must stop
Q211073.s: Matadi clings to steep, rocky hills on the left bank of the Congo, about 150 km from the Atlantic. It is as far as ocean-going ships can sail: just upstream, the river squeezes into gorges and rapids. In the 1890s a railway was built to carry goods around them to Kinshasa. The town's name means 'stones' in Kikongo.
Q211073.w: A hilly, rocky town on a narrow, fast stretch of the Congo, crossed by a single long suspension bridge.
f: The Matadi–Kinshasa railway, built between 1890 and 1898, bypasses the Livingstone Falls.
The Matadi Bridge over the Congo has a main span of about 520 metres.
Upstream at Yelala Falls, the Portuguese navigator Diogo Cão left an inscription on the rocks in 1485.

q.q: What does the name Matadi mean in Kikongo?

Q271404.t: A mining town ringed by giant open pits
Q271404.s: Kolwezi sits on a high plateau in the south of the Congo, on one of the richest mineral belts on Earth. From above, the land around the town is scarred by huge open-pit mines: terraced craters, grey spoil heaps and pale tailings ponds. The ores here carry copper and cobalt, a metal now in demand for rechargeable batteries.
Q271404.w: A town surrounded by vast terraced open-pit mines, grey spoil heaps and flat tailings ponds on a high plateau.
f: The Democratic Republic of the Congo produces more than half of the world's mined cobalt, much of it around Kolwezi.
The Central African Copperbelt stretches from Kolwezi across the border into Zambia.
Kolwezi lies about 1,450 metres above sea level.

q.q: Which battery metal is mined in large amounts around Kolwezi?

Q187593.t: Copper capital with a black mountain of slag
Q187593.s: Lubumbashi spreads across the high, flat plateau of the Copperbelt in the far south-east of the Congo, only a few dozen kilometres from Zambia. Look for a dark hill near the city centre: a huge heap of slag left by a century of copper smelting, beside the smelter's tall chimney. The city was founded in 1910 as Élisabethville.
Q187593.w: A grid-planned city on a flat plateau, with a dark, flat-topped slag heap near its centre and dry woodland around.
f: Lubumbashi is one of the largest cities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The Zambian border lies only some 30 km away.
Miombo woodland, a dry forest of broad-leaved trees, covers much of the plateau around the city.

q.q: What was Lubumbashi called when it was founded in 1910?

Q3876.t: A garden capital spread across the central plateau
Q3876.s: Lilongwe lies on Malawi's central plateau, about 1,050 metres up, a spread-out city of separate districts divided by green belts and the winding Lilongwe River. Around it, red soil and farmland stretch in every direction, much of it planted with maize and tobacco. About 100 km to the east, the land drops to the shore of Lake Malawi.
Q3876.w: A loose, spread-out city of separate districts among trees and red farmland, crossed by a small winding river.
f: Lilongwe replaced Zomba as Malawi's capital in 1975.
Lake Malawi is home to more species of fish than any other lake on Earth.
Many of Lilongwe's neighbourhoods have numbers instead of names, such as Area 3 or Area 47.

q.q: Which lake lies about 100 km east of Lilongwe?

Q3825.t: A 'free town' on an estuary just north of the equator
Q3825.s: Libreville lies on the north shore of the Komo estuary, where the river opens into the Atlantic, only about 40 km north of the equator. Rainforest reaches almost to the city's edge, and across the estuary the mangroves and beaches of Pongara National Park stay wild. The city was founded in 1849 by freed Africans rescued from a slave ship.
Q3825.w: A city along the north shore of a wide estuary opening to the sea, with dense green forest and mangroves on the far side.
f: The beaches of Pongara, across the estuary, are a nesting ground for leatherback turtles.
Close to 90 percent of Gabon is covered by forest.
Libreville is Gabon's capital and by far its largest city.

q.q: What does the name Libreville mean?

Q501715.t: An island oil town on the edge of a great delta
Q501715.s: Port-Gentil stands near the tip of Cape Lopez on Mandji Island, a flat, sandy island at the mouth of the Ogooué, Gabon's great river. Behind it spreads the river's delta, a maze of channels, lagoons and mangroves. The town is the centre of Gabon's oil industry, and at night you may spot the lights of offshore platforms out in the Atlantic.
Q501715.w: A small town on the northern tip of a flat, sandy island, with a vast delta of channels and mangroves to the south-east.
f: The Ogooué is Gabon's longest river, draining most of the country.
Cape Lopez is named after the Portuguese navigator Lopo Gonçalves, who sailed past it in the 1470s.

q.q: At the mouth of which river does Port-Gentil stand?

Q9427.t: The fabled desert city, just beyond the Niger
Q9427.s: Timbuktu stands where desert meets river: the Sahara's sand reaches its northern edge, while the Niger flows about 15 km to the south. From above, it is a small, sand-coloured town that could be anywhere. Yet from the 14th to the 16th centuries it was a great centre of trade and Islamic scholarship, its libraries filled with manuscripts.
Q9427.w: A small, sand-coloured town on the edge of dunes, with the green floodplain of the Niger a short way to the south.
f: The Djinguereyber Mosque, built around 1327, is made largely of mud and straw.
Families in Timbuktu have kept tens of thousands of old manuscripts on law, astronomy and medicine.
Timbuktu has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1988.

q.q: Which Mali emperor had Timbuktu's Djinguereyber Mosque built?

Q3688.t: A desert capital built on the dunes by the Atlantic
Q3688.s: Nouakchott lies where the Sahara meets the Atlantic, a low, sprawling city on flat sand between the ocean and a sea of dunes. It was little more than a village when work began in 1958 on a new capital, planned for about 15,000 people. Today it is home to around a million, and the desert still presses against its edges.
Q3688.w: A low, sprawling city on flat sand, a straight Atlantic beach to the west and orange dunes pressing in from the east.
f: Banc d'Arguin National Park, a UNESCO site up the coast, hosts millions of wintering shorebirds.
Much of the city lies only a few metres above sea level.
The name Nouakchott is often translated as 'place of the winds'.

q.q: In which year did work begin on Nouakchott as a new capital?

Q3703.t: A capital on the Niger beneath a sandstone escarpment
Q3703.s: Bamako spreads along both banks of the Niger, a wide, shallow river braided with sandbanks and small rocky islands. Behind the city to the north rises the edge of the Manding Plateau, a line of sandstone cliffs and hills. Bridges tie the two halves of the city together. The name is often said to mean 'crocodile river' in Bambara.
Q3703.w: A broad city on both banks of a wide river with sandbanks and bridges, backed by sandstone hills to the north.
f: Just downstream of the centre, the Sotuba rapids break the flow of the Niger.
Bamako is one of the fastest-growing cities in Africa.
The Niger rises only about 250 km from the Atlantic, yet flows inland, away from it, past Bamako.

q.q: What is Bamako's name often said to mean?

Q735645.t: An oasis gateway to the Adrar and the Eye of the Sahara
Q735645.s: Atar is an oasis town of date palms in a valley of the Adrar plateau, in the heart of the Mauritanian Sahara. Dark sandstone cliffs and orange dunes surround it. Some 180 km to the north-east lies one of the most famous sights seen from the air: the Richat Structure, or Eye of the Sahara, a vast set of concentric rock rings.
Q735645.w: A green strip of palm groves in a dry valley between dark plateau cliffs, with sand dunes spreading around.
f: The Richat Structure is about 40 km across, big enough to be picked out by astronauts.
Chinguetti, an old caravan town about 80 km to the east, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Every summer the date harvest, the guetna, draws families to the oases of the Adrar.

q.q: What is the Eye of the Sahara, north-east of Atar?
q.a: An eroded dome of rock layers

Q213507.t: A mud-brick town that becomes an island in the flood
Q213507.s: Djenné stands in the inland delta of the Niger, on a patch of higher ground that the Bani River's floods turn into an island each rainy season. Its Great Mosque is the largest mud-brick building in the world, and every year the townspeople replaster it together in a festival. From above, look for a compact brown town ringed by water or green floodplain.
Q213507.w: A compact, earth-brown town on a low island in a wide, flat floodplain that turns to water in the wet season.
f: The present Great Mosque dates from 1907, rebuilt on the site of a much older mosque.
Nearby Djenné-Djeno, settled around 250 BC, is one of the oldest known towns in sub-Saharan Africa.
The old towns of Djenné have been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1988.

q.q: What do Djenné's people replaster together every year?

Q208389.t: A Sahara oasis city with green circles in the sand
Q208389.s: Sabha lies deep in the Libyan Sahara, in the Fezzan, a region of sand seas, stony plateaus and strings of oases. From above, look for perfect green circles in the desert around it: fields watered by rotating irrigation arms that draw on ancient groundwater. For centuries the town was a crossroads for caravans between the Mediterranean and the Sahel.
Q208389.w: A town on a flat desert plain, with scattered green circular fields and dark rocky plateaus and sand seas around.
f: The groundwater pumped around Sabha fell as rain thousands of years ago, when the Sahara was greener.
About 150 km to the west, Germa was the capital of the Garamantes, a desert kingdom of Roman times.
Many years pass in the Fezzan with almost no rain at all.

q.q: Which ancient people ruled a desert kingdom west of Sabha?

Q40816.t: A Greek-founded port on the Gulf of Sidra
Q40816.s: Benghazi spreads along a low coast at the north-eastern corner of the Gulf of Sidra, where salt marshes and lagoons edge the sea. Inland to the east rise the green uplands of the Jebel Akhdar, one of the wettest parts of Libya. The city began as the Greek colony of Euesperides and was later renamed Berenice, after a Ptolemaic queen.
Q40816.w: A flat coastal city with lagoons and salt flats along the shore, and a green, wooded upland rising to the north-east.
f: Greek settlers founded Euesperides here in the 6th century BC.
The Jebel Akhdar, the 'Green Mountain', gets far more rain than almost anywhere else in Libya.
Benghazi is Libya's second-largest city.

q.q: What was Benghazi called in Ptolemaic times?

Q17151.t: A port city facing Mount Olympus across the gulf
Q17151.s: Thessaloniki curves along the head of the Thermaic Gulf, a long waterfront backed by hills. On a clear day, look south-west across the water: the massif of Mount Olympus, home of the Greek gods, rises to nearly 3,000 metres, often capped with snow. West of the city, the Axios River builds a green delta of wetlands and rice fields.
Q17151.w: A city along the curving head of a gulf, backed by hills, with a river delta to the west and Olympus across the water.
f: King Cassander founded the city in 315 BC and named it after his wife Thessalonike, half-sister of Alexander the Great.
Mount Olympus reaches about 2,918 metres, the highest point in Greece.
The city's early Christian and Byzantine monuments are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: Thessaloniki is named after the half-sister of which ruler?

Q3820.t: A city on a cape, with snowy mountains at its back
Q3820.s: Beirut sits on a triangular cape pushing into the Mediterranean, with the slopes of Mount Lebanon rising steeply just behind it. In winter the peaks, well over 2,000 metres high, turn white with snow while the sea below stays blue. Off the western tip stand two great sea arches, the Pigeon Rocks. As Roman Berytus, the city was famous for its school of law.
Q3820.w: A dense city covering a triangular cape, with steep mountain slopes rising immediately inland to the east.
f: Beirut has been inhabited for around 5,000 years.
The cedar is Lebanon's emblem, and old cedar groves survive high on Mount Lebanon.
In late winter it is possible to ski on Mount Lebanon and swim in the sea on the same day.

q.q: What kind of school made Roman Berytus famous?

Q994.t: A city named for its warm springs, in a river gorge
Q994.s: Tbilisi winds along the valley of the Kura, which cuts through the city in a narrow gorge between steep hills. The old town clusters beneath a fortress on a ridge, where hot sulphur springs still feed domed bathhouses. The name comes from the Georgian word for 'warm'. On clear days the snowy wall of the Greater Caucasus stands along the northern horizon.
Q994.w: A long city in a winding river valley between bare hills, with the snowy Greater Caucasus range far to the north.
f: King Vakhtang Gorgasali is traditionally credited with founding the city in the 5th century.
The Tbilisi Sea, a reservoir on the city's north-eastern edge, is about 9 km long.
The Kura, called the Mtkvari in Georgian, flows on to the Caspian Sea through Azerbaijan.

q.q: What gave Tbilisi its name?

Q218861.t: A castle-studded royal city above Lake Tana
Q218861.s: Gondar sits on the northern Ethiopian Highlands at over 2,100 metres, on hills overlooking the plain that runs down to Lake Tana, some 35 km to the south. In 1636 Emperor Fasilides made it his capital and built a stone castle; his successors added more, forming a walled royal enclosure. To the north-east rise the jagged Simien Mountains.
Q218861.w: A hilly town on the highlands with a large lake to the south and a range of jagged peaks far to the north-east.
f: The royal enclosure of Fasil Ghebbi has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1979.
Gondar remained Ethiopia's capital for more than two centuries.
The Simien Mountains include Ras Dashen, at about 4,550 metres Ethiopia's highest peak.

q.q: Which lake, source of the Blue Nile, lies south of Gondar?
